01 · Position

sections.heading: One sentence.
sections.text:
The position

We build design systems that work for both humans and AI tools — structured platforms that help product teams ship faster, govern brand and accessibility at scale, and bring AI into design and development with predictable, on-brand output.

This works for two kinds of clients. Those who already use AI tools and want better output. And those who are introducing AI into their delivery and need the system ready for it. Both engagements end with the same thing — a design system the AI tools can actually use.

sections.heading: Where this offering ends, and where it starts small
sections.text:
This portfolio is design systems work. Adjacent engagements — brand identity refreshes, broader AI strategy consulting, standalone Figma libraries, productized SaaS — sit with other Nagarro practices or run as separate scopes.

Smaller foot-in-the-door engagements are welcome. AI tooling POCs, AI-readiness assessments, targeted component packages, and AI strategy advisory can all run as small starter scopes that lead into Diagnose. The Vorwerk engagement is a recent example — we introduced AI into the client's process, prepared the design system to be AI-Ready, and shipped a working POC before scoping anything larger.

02 · Why now

sections.heading: AI tools are at enterprise scale.
sections.text: Cursor, Claude, Copilot, and v0 are standard issue at most product organisations of meaningful size. Output quality is the next conversation, not adoption.

sections.heading: Design system maturity has split.
sections.text: A small number of organisations have mature systems. Most have a 2020-vintage Figma library and a Confluence page that hasn't been updated. The 2020-vintage system is the worst possible starting point for AI consumption.

sections.heading: The technical primitives are mature.
sections.text:
Tokens Studio, Style Dictionary, Figma Dev Mode MCP, Figma Code Connect, Storybook with MCP integration — all stable, all deployable. The work is integration and governance, not invention.

Offer 01 · Diagnose

Diagnose

A two-week paid assessment that tells you what kind of design system investment will actually move your business — and what it will cost.

How to pitch: Two weeks, eight thousand euros, binding recommendation. If the answer is "don't engage," that's what we tell you. Most buyers find it refreshing.

Most design system conversations stall because the buyer can't quantify the problem.

Diagnose produces the numbers and a binding recommendation. If the right answer is "do nothing for six months," we say so. Paid diagnostics produce binding recommendations. Free ones produce free-quality work.

Who this is for

- — Product or engineering leaders who suspect their design system is costing them velocity but can't put a number on it.

- — Leaders whose teams have rolled out AI coding tools and aren't happy with the output.

- — Leaders about to introduce AI into their delivery, who want to know what's in their way.

How AI is used in Diagnose

Vision models catalogue production screens against the existing component library and flag duplicates and orphans. AI inspects Figma libraries for structural issues — missing tokens, inconsistent variant strategies, components built outside the library, accessibility gaps. Static analysis plus LLM-assisted categorisation maps token use across the front-end code. We run a round-trip test: real prompts go through Cursor, Claude, and Copilot against the current system, scored on brand match, accessibility, token use, and naming.

What we deliver

-
Product and design system audit
Two to four products, screen-level cataloguing of component usage, token coverage, accessibility findings, responsive coverage, and pattern duplication.

-
Figma and tooling audit
Component structure, token use, Figma library hygiene, variant strategy, Storybook presence and quality, code-component parity, CI checks. How designers and developers actually work today — not how they say they work.

-
Design-to-code workflow review
How Figma decisions move into code, where the breakage points are, and where AI tools fit or don't.

-
Maturity score
Token, component, documentation, governance, accessibility, AI-readiness — scored on a defined rubric, comparable across engagements.

-
Cost-of-fragmentation estimate
A model of engineering and design rework attributable to system gaps. A defensible estimate, not an audit.

-
Recommended path
One of: Launch, Unify, Supercharge, a combination, or no engagement.

Offer 02 · Launch

Launch

Build a new product and its design system together, so the system is in place before fragmentation begins.

How to pitch: Build the design system at the same time as the first product, while the cost of getting it right is cheapest. A small AI-proficient team does the work that used to need twice the headcount.

New product builds have a window — usually 6 to 12 months — when retrofitting a design system is cheap.

After that window closes, every component that ships without a system entry becomes technical debt. We build the system alongside the product, with a small AI-proficient team that does the work that used to need twice the headcount.

Who this is for

- — Teams building a new product, platform, market entry, or proposition.

- — Post-MVP scale moments. Product-market fit is real, the next 50 features need to ship without the codebase falling apart.

- — Post-acquisition new-product builds with no inherited system.

How AI is used in Launch

AI generates the variant matrix from the base components designers create — then designers review every variant before it ships. AI authors prose documentation from human-authored structured metadata. CI agents check spacing, contrast, naming, accessibility, and token use on every pull request. Figma Dev Mode MCP plus Code Connect means design and code share the same notion of a component, queryable by AI tools in either direction.

Component library across Figma and code

Offer 03 · Unify

Unify

Consolidate a fragmented product ecosystem into one governed system, with controlled variation where the business needs it.

How to pitch: You don't need consistency. You need controlled variation. We define what stays shared and what can vary, so teams move independently without the product drifting apart.

Fragmentation is rarely one decision. It's the cumulative result of many small reasonable decisions made by independent teams.

Trying to un-make those decisions one at a time fails. The win is to define what must be shared (tokens, primitives, accessibility, semantic naming), what can vary (composition, marketing surfaces, regional adaptations), and what should be one-off (campaign overlays, experiments). That's controlled variation — a more honest promise than consistency.

Who this is for

- — Multi-product, multi-brand, multi-platform organisations where teams have drifted.

- — Post-merger and post-acquisition portfolios.

- — Organisations with two-to-five Figma libraries that nobody keeps in sync.

- — Enterprises where governance has been deferred for years.

How AI is used in Unify

Vision models classify screens against the existing library and flag duplicates and orphans. AI-assisted mapping links legacy components to the unified library with confidence scores, so reviewers focus on the ambiguous cases. AI-generated codemods handle class-of-changes (renamed tokens, restructured components), reviewed by engineers before they run. Governance agents review pull requests against system rules.

What we deliver

Experience and component audit
Multi-product, screen-level. Code-level where access permits. Shared, variable, and one-off patterns identified.

Controlled-variation architecture
Token taxonomy that supports multi-brand and multi-platform variation. Component composition rules: locked, parameterisable, replaceable.

-
Migration plan

-
Federated contribution model
RFC process, contribution workflow, review requirements. Defines what gets centralised and what stays distributed.

-
Governance automation
Linting, token validation, conformance checks, visual regression CI, accessibility CI.

-
Adoption tooling
Telemetry: components used where, products on which version, exceptions open.

Offer 04 · Supercharge

Supercharge

Restructure the system so generative AI tools produce on-brand, accessible, governed output — whether you're already using AI tools or about to introduce them.

How to pitch: If your engineers are getting generic output from Cursor or Claude, we make the system AI-readable and prove it with a working POC. If you're about to introduce AI tools, we set them up against your standards before you scale. That is what we did at Vorwerk.

Two scenarios, same engagement.

First: organisations whose design system works for humans but whose AI coding output is generic. Engineers spend half their time fixing the generated code. Second: organisations about to bring AI into their delivery, who want a working POC before enterprise rollout. The Vorwerk engagement is the recent example of the second case — we introduced AI tools, prepared the system, and shipped a POC that demonstrated AI-assisted design and code working with the client's brand and standards.

Who this is for

- — Organisations whose design system works for humans but whose AI output is generic.

- — Organisations that have rolled out Cursor, Copilot, Claude, or v0 at scale.

- — Organisations about to introduce AI into design and development, who want to do it cleanly the first time.

- — Engineering leaders whose teams "love the AI tools but spend half the time fixing the output."

How AI is used in Supercharge

AI proposes structured metadata from existing code and Figma; humans verify. Prose documentation is generated from metadata, then reviewed. The validation harness runs continuous AI-assisted comparison of generated output against system rules. Every designer and engineer on the engagement uses AI tools as part of their daily work — we do not staff a separate AI specialist.

ICP 01

sections.heading: Enterprise Multi-Brand Product Organisations
sections.text:
1,500+ employees. Multiple product lines, multiple brands or white-label customer skins. Platform engineering, design ops, and accessibility programmes already at some maturity. Densest in insurance, financial services, healthcare, retail, manufacturing, telecoms, regulated infrastructure.

Buying triggers

- Executive complaint that the portfolio feels inconsistent to customers and analysts.

- Planned brand consolidation or platform modernisation.

- Accessibility compliance pressure (e.g. European Accessibility Act).

- AI coding tool rollout with visible output-quality complaints.

- New CTO or CPO inheriting a fragmented portfolio.

Pain hierarchy

- Brand drift creates analyst and customer complaints.

- Engineering velocity drops as teams reimplement primitives.

- Accessibility audit findings are inconsistent across products.

- AI tooling investment shows no measurable productivity gain.

- Design system team is too small for product demand.

Decision unit
Economic buyer: CPO or CTO (CIO in regulated sectors). Champion: Head of Design / DesignOps / Platform Engineering. Technical evaluator: Principal frontend engineer or platform architect. Blocker risk: Procurement, security, legal.

Evidence to lead with
Datto. ADT. Moody's RMS.

Disqualifiers

- Active M&A or carve-out making the portfolio unstable.

- No executive sponsor for governance enforcement.

- Recent failed engagement with another vendor (under 18 months).

Recommended path
Diagnose→Unify·+ Supercharge Y2

ICP 02

sections.heading: Scale-up Platform Companies
sections.text:
200–1,500 employees. Series B+ to pre-IPO. B2B SaaS, dev tools, vertical SaaS, or platform plays. Rapid product expansion, often two-to-five new products planned. Engineering culture, AI-tool-positive, hires fast.

Buying triggers

- New funding round and stated platform-expansion strategy.

- Hire of first Head of Design or first Head of DesignOps.

- Sales-demo-visible inconsistency between flagship and new products.

- Cursor or Copilot rollout producing generic output.

- Pre-IPO or pre-acquisition design due diligence.

Pain hierarchy

- Engineering velocity is the KPI and the system is slowing it down.

- New product lines look like different companies' products.

- AI tools produce output that doesn't match the flagship.

- Engineer onboarding is slow because patterns aren't documented.

- "System owner" is no one in particular.

Decision unit
Economic buyer: VP Engineering, Head of Design, or CTO. CEO often involved. Champion: Head of Design or staff frontend engineer. Technical evaluator: Lead frontend engineer. Blocker risk: Velocity culture.

Evidence to lead with
Securra. Moody's RMS.

Disqualifiers

- Pre-product-market-fit.

- Single product, single team, under 30 engineers.

- No identified system owner on the client side.

ICP 03

sections.heading: Post-Merger and Carve-Out Product Consolidation
sections.text:
Organisations in M&A integration, carve-out from a parent, or major business-unit consolidation. May span any size but with the urgency and budget of a transformation programme. Densest in PE portfolio integrations, financial services M&A, healthcare consolidations, tech-sector acquisitions.

Buying triggers

- Announced M&A or carve-out with a 12–24 month integration deadline.

- Customer-facing brand consolidation announcement.

- Cost-synergy targets requiring platform consolidation.

- Regulatory pressure to standardise compliance-bearing UI.

Pain hierarchy

- Two or more design systems can't run in parallel forever.

- Engineering teams use different toolchains — usually the hidden blocker.

- Brand alignment has a hard deadline.

- Cost synergies assume efficiency gains that depend on consolidation.

Decision unit
Economic buyer: Integration programme leadership, often CIO or COO of the new entity. Champion: Integration programme manager, head of platform, head of digital. Technical evaluator: Architects from both sides. Blocker risk: Politics.

Evidence to lead with
Datto. Any PE portfolio harmonisation we can name.

Disqualifiers

- Integration deadline under 6 months.

- No neutral executive sponsor.

- Integration scope still being negotiated.

Recommended path
Diagnose→Unify

ICP 04

sections.heading: AI Transformation Programmes
sections.text:
Organisations whose stated strategy includes AI as a productivity multiplier. Any size, most commonly enterprise. Rolling out AI coding tools or about to introduce them. Often board-level mandate to show productivity gains. Densest in financial services, technology, professional services, regulated software.

Buying triggers

- Published AI strategy with productivity targets.

- Enterprise rollout of Cursor, Claude, Copilot above 500 seats.

- Output-quality complaints from engineering managers.

- AI investment review where productivity gains aren't visible.

- New CTO or Chief AI Officer reviewing the tooling estate.

- Decision to introduce AI tools and a need to do it cleanly the first time.

Pain hierarchy

- AI tools paid for, output is generic, off-brand, or non-compliant.

- Engineers spend more time fixing AI output than writing code.

- The design system isn't consumable by AI tools.

- Governance has no automated enforcement; AI output bypasses review.

- Brand and accessibility regressions in AI-generated code.

Decision unit
Economic buyer: CTO, Chief AI Officer, or VP Engineering. Champion: Head of platform, developer experience, or design. Technical evaluator: Principal engineer in the AI-tooling or platform team. Blocker risk: Security, legal.

Vorwerk. Internal Nagarro AI-assisted SDLC.

- AI adoption still pilot-stage with no commitment to scale.

- Design system unstable. Run Launch or Unify first.

sections.heading: Discovery questions
sections.text:
Use these in the first qualifying call.

- How many design system libraries are in active use across your products?

- Where do design decisions get reinterpreted between Figma and production code?

- Which teams are already using AI tools for design or code? What does the output look like compared to your standards?

- Where do brand, accessibility, or compliance issues usually get caught — design review, code review, or production?

- Who owns contribution, approval, versioning, and adoption today?

- What happens when a new product, store, or campaign needs to launch — does it slot into the system, or does it become an exception?

- If we ran a two-week diagnostic, who would be in the room with us on your side?

sections.heading: Common objections and responses
sections.text:
"We already have a design system."
That's why Diagnose exists. Two weeks, fixed price. We test whether the system is AI-ready and whether it covers what you're shipping next. If it is healthy, the engagement ends there.

"We can build this internally."
Many clients do. We help when the internal team is one or two people and the system needs to scale faster than hiring allows. Most clients pair us with their internal hire — we accelerate the system, they own it long-term.

"AI tools will solve this for us automatically."
AI tools need context. The design system is the context. Without structure, the tools produce generic output that engineers spend half their time fixing. The investment is in the system, not the tools.

"This is too expensive."
Diagnose is eight thousand euros. Full Launch is from eighty-one thousand. Comparable internal effort — one design system architect and one senior engineer for two months — is roughly the same loaded cost, without the tooling, governance, or AI integration we bring.

"Why not just hire a head of design systems?"
That hire is the right move and we can help scope the role. The system you hand to that person matters more than the hire alone — and the ongoing work runs as T&M while they ramp up.

"The MCP server has to live on our infrastructure."
That's our default. We deploy to client infra. We do not host long-term.

"We don't have an executive sponsor yet."
Then it is too early. Diagnose needs one. We can run a smaller scoping conversation, but we won't open a full diagnostic without sponsor commitment.

10 · Methodology

sections.heading: Six phases, collapsed differently per offer.
sections.text:
Phase · What happens ·

Discover · Brief, decision unit, success criteria. Always paid. Always time-boxed. ·

Architect · System architecture: tokens, components, metadata, governance, integrations. ·

Build · Implementation. Iterative against real client product flows. ·

Integrate · Connect to design tools (Figma, Code Connect, Tokens Studio), code tools (Storybook, packages, CI), AI tools (MCP server, Cursor, Claude, Copilot, validation harness). ·

Adopt · Roll out to client teams: training, contribution model, governance enforcement, telemetry. ·

Continue · Ongoing T&M support: component delivery, governance, telemetry, training, AI-tool integration upkeep. ·

Diagnose runs Discover alone. Launch and Unify run Discover through Adopt. Supercharge runs Discover through Integrate with a validation-focused Adopt. Continue is T&M at €85 per hour blended.

sections.heading: What AI does as part of the team
sections.text:
AI is part of the working team, not a tool the team picks up occasionally. On every engagement it does substantive design and engineering work that would historically have taken human time:

Component creationCreates components in Figma based on system rules — variants, states, responsive behaviour. Creates the equivalent code components with the right props, tokens, and accessibility primitives.
Token workGenerates and refactors design tokens, including platform-specific outputs via Style Dictionary.
AccessibilityAudits and improves accessibility — colour contrast, focus order, ARIA usage, screen-reader behaviour.
UsabilityAudits and improves usability — interaction patterns, copy clarity, error states.
Issue identificationIdentifies issues in component structure, missing tokens, naming inconsistencies, and library drift.
DocumentationWrites and updates prose documentation from the structured metadata layer.
QA & CIRuns validation in CI: visual regression, accessibility, naming, token use.

What AI does not do: replace the design systems team. The team owns strategy, governance, exceptions, releases, and the final call on every decision. AI does the work the team would otherwise be doing manually.
